questions.title: What can a court consider on a Rule 12 motion to dismiss an indictment for failure to state an offense?
questions.question_body: The Fifth Circuit says it reviews the sufficiency of an indictment de novo and must take the allegations as true, citing Rafoi and Fontenot. The district court dismissed for not alleging deprivation of a traditional property interest. I'm confused about the scope of what the district court could look at. On a Rule 12(b)(3)(B)(v) motion, can the court consider evidence that investors received market-value securities or that the posts were opinions/puffery, or is it strictly confined to the four corners of the indictment? When (if ever) can a court resolve factual disputes pretrial in this posture?

questions.title: How exactly does the 'fraudulent-inducement' theory differ from the rejected 'right-to-control' theory, and why does it fit a pump-and-dump?
questions.question_body: The panel says Ciminelli bars convictions based solely on depriving victims of 'valuable economic information,' but Kousisis approves the 'fraudulent-inducement' theory where a lie tricks the victim into a transaction that requires handing over money or property. In this pump-and-dump, the defendants allegedly misrepresented positions/price targets, followers bought, and defendants sold. Is the object here truly to 'obtain the victim's money' even though the victims got stock in return? Does it matter if the defendants didn't sell directly to their followers but into the market generally? How does that distinction play into the fraudulent-inducement framing?

questions.title: Does § 1348(1) require that obtaining 'money or property' be an object of the scheme, or is that only in § 1348(2)?
questions.question_body: Section 1348 has two clauses: (1) schemes to defraud in connection with a security, and (2) schemes to obtain money or property by false pretenses in connection with a security. The opinion repeatedly frames the elements as deception plus 'obtaining the victim’s money or property' being an object, relying on Kousisis. Is the court effectively importing a money-or-property objective into § 1348(1) as well? Is there any authority or circuit split on whether subsection (1) stands on its own without an 'obtain money or property' requirement?

questions.title: After Kousisis, does 'intent to defraud' require an intent to cause loss, or is intent to obtain money enough?
questions.question_body: The defendants argued they only intended to profit, not harm anyone, but the panel says that's a distinction without a difference under Kousisis and cites that actual loss isn't required. Under Fifth Circuit law (Evans) and Kousisis, what exactly satisfies the 'intent to defraud' element? If a defendant believes the counterparty will receive equivalent value (e.g., stock at then-market price) or might even profit later, can 'intent to defraud' still be shown solely by intent to deceive and to obtain money via that deceit?

questions.title: Are social-media statements about one's trading positions and 'price targets' material misrepresentations under § 1348, or are they puffery/opinion?
questions.question_body: The indictment alleges the defendants misrepresented their positions and potential prices to induce purchases. Are statements like 'I'm buying' or 'this could go to $10' considered actionable misrepresentations of fact for criminal securities fraud, or could they be non-actionable puffery/opinion? Does the Omnicare framework for opinion statements in securities cases apply in criminal § 1348 prosecutions, and what would make a 'price target' or 'I'm buying' statement materially false or misleading in this context?

questions.title: What must the government show about 'in connection with' the purchase or sale—do the deceived buyers have to be the defendants’ counterparties?
questions.question_body: The court treats the followers as victims who were induced to purchase, and the defendants as having obtained money from the scheme. In a dispersed market, however, induced buyers might purchase from other sellers, while defendants might dump to different buyers. For § 1348 liability, must the government prove the defendants obtained money specifically from the deceived purchasers, or is it enough that the scheme involved lies that induced market transactions in the relevant securities, during which the defendants monetized their positions?

questions.title: Do reliance, price impact, or loss causation play any role in a criminal § 1348 case compared to Rule 10b-5?
questions.question_body: In civil 10b-5, plaintiffs must prove reliance, loss causation, and economic loss. This opinion suggests actual loss isn't required for § 1348 and focuses on scheme and intent to defraud. In a criminal § 1348 prosecution like this one, do the government and jury need to find investor reliance or price impact? If not, what evidentiary showings typically substitute for those civil elements to establish materiality and causation in the criminal context?

questions.title: How far can courts 'borrow' mail/wire fraud concepts to interpret § 1348, and are there limits to that approach?
questions.question_body: The panel notes 'scant caselaw' on § 1348 and says courts borrow key concepts from mail and wire fraud. Is there Supreme Court or Fifth Circuit guidance on the propriety and limits of this borrowing? Could relying too heavily on mail/wire fraud doctrines (like Kousisis or Evans) risk importing elements or defenses that don't fit the text or structure of § 1348, which also sits alongside Rule 10b-5? Where have courts drawn boundaries on this analogical approach?
